paragraphs: Subspace-preserving recovery asks whether a data point can be represented using points from its own underlying subspace. This question supports methods for grouping or classifying data drawn from several subspaces. Existing theory largely offered sufficient conditions: satisfying them guaranteed success, but failing them did not establish failure.

The paper introduces a subspace nullspace property that is both necessary and sufficient for recovery. Inspired by a corresponding idea in sparse recovery, it gives an exact characterization rather than only a collection of safe cases. The authors develop equivalent formulations that explain recovery geometrically through the distribution of data and the separation between subspaces.

Another formulation can be checked using finitely many extreme points of a suitable set. The authors also derive new sufficient conditions involving inner and outer radii and dual bounds. These extend existing conditions while retaining geometric meaning. Together, the results connect an exact mathematical criterion to more interpretable ways of understanding when recovery succeeds.
icml-2021-a-nullspace-property-for-subsp.tldr: A new necessary and sufficient condition characterizes subspace-preserving recovery and yields geometric interpretations and broader sufficient guarantees.

paragraphs: Active covering starts with an unlabeled dataset and lets a learner request labels sequentially. Its objective is to query every positive example while spending as few total label queries as possible. The central issue is therefore how to direct labeling effort toward positive examples without overlooking those that remain.

Under standard nonparametric assumptions, the authors first repurpose a classical support estimator as an offline method. Its excess query cost relative to the optimal learner scales as n raised to D/(D+1), up to logarithmic factors, where n is dataset size and D is dimension. Their active method improves the upper bound to n raised to (D−1)/D, again suppressing logarithmic factors.

These bounds measure additional queries beyond the optimal learner's cost, rather than total labeling effort. The algorithms require access only to positively labeled examples, which can bring computational and privacy benefits in some settings. On a broad range of image benchmarks, the active method consistently outperformed the evaluated offline methods and other baselines, supporting the value of sequentially directing queries.
icml-2021-active-covering-08bf7d6080.tldr: An active labeling method improves theoretical excess-query bounds and empirical performance when searching for every positive example in a dataset.

paragraphs: Learning reusable skills from long demonstrations is difficult when the demonstrations do not identify which skill is active at each point. A hierarchical imitation learner must infer this structure while also learning behavior. The paper addresses this joint problem with Option-GAIL, motivated by compounding errors and suboptimal solutions in existing approaches.

Option-GAIL represents the task hierarchy using options and trains through generative adversarial optimization. Its learning procedure alternates between two steps in the style of expectation-maximization. The first samples possible expert options conditioned on the currently learned policy. The second updates the agent's high-level and low-level policies together.

Those updates minimize a proposed discrepancy in option occupancy between expert and agent, bringing the inferred skill hierarchy into the imitation objective. This makes skill inference and policy learning parts of the same alternating procedure. The authors prove convergence of their algorithm and report consistent improvements over comparison methods across several tasks. The convergence result concerns the proposed procedure; the reported task advantages are empirical findings.
icml-2021-adversarial-option-aware-hiera.tldr: Option-GAIL jointly infers expert options and learns hierarchical policies through an adversarial imitation procedure with a convergence proof.

paragraphs: Batched bandit learning balances two costs: losses from choosing inferior arms and the number of batches used to organize decisions. Many existing methods require the total number of decisions in advance. This paper studies an anytime setting, where the learner must operate without knowing when the process will stop.

For reward distributions in exponential families, the authors propose an anytime algorithm with asymptotically optimal regret. Its batch count is bounded by log log T multiplied by an iterated logarithm of T. An iterated logarithm means applying the logarithm repeatedly, with the number of applications held constant as the horizon T grows.

The paper also establishes a lower bound: in the studied setting, no algorithm can achieve asymptotically optimal regret using at most c times log log T batches for any fixed positive constant c. Thus, the extra slowly growing factor in the proposed bound addresses a real obstruction. The result explains how nearly optimal batching can coexist with optimal long-run regret when the stopping time is unknown.
icml-2021-almost-optimal-anytime-algorit.tldr: An anytime batched bandit algorithm achieves asymptotically optimal regret with a batch count close to a proved lower bound.

paragraphs: The paper asks how efficiently convolutional architectures can represent relationships in time series. It treats this as functional approximation: a model tries to reproduce a target relationship involving temporal data. WaveNet is a principal example of the architecture family considered, while the contribution is a theoretical analysis of approximation properties.

Earlier results for recurrent architectures connected approximation efficiency to the memory structure of the process generating the data. The authors derive corresponding results for convolutional architectures, but find that memory alone does not characterize their approximation efficiency. Finer structure within the target temporal relationship also matters.

To express that additional structure, the paper introduces a spectrum-based notion of regularity. This measures the complexity of temporal relationships specifically under the convolutional approximation scheme. The analysis therefore gives a mathematical basis for understanding why architecture choice matters even when temporal memory is taken into account. It can inform practical choices by relating model architecture to properties of the relationship being modeled.
icml-2021-approximation-theory-of-convol.tldr: Convolutional time-series approximation depends on both memory and finer temporal structure, captured by a new spectrum-based regularity measure.

paragraphs: A highly flexible model can learn patterns shared by many examples while also memorizing unusual cases. This paper examines that distinction at the level of individual labeled examples. Its goal is to characterize how regularly an example fits the patterns a model learns from other data.

The authors introduce a consistency score based on expected prediction accuracy for a held-out example across training sets of varying sizes sampled from the data distribution. Holding the example out makes the score about learning from related observations. Varying the training data reveals how reliably the example can be predicted from those observations.

Empirical estimates across multiple datasets place mislabeled and out-of-distribution examples toward one end of the score continuum and strongly regular examples toward the other. The authors also identify inexpensive proxies using statistics gathered during training. They apply the score to investigate representation-learning dynamics and to filter training outliers, connecting an instance-level measure of regularity to both model analysis and data handling.
icml-2021-characterizing-structural-regu.tldr: An instance-level consistency score distinguishes shared learnable structure from irregular examples and supports representation analysis and outlier filtering.

paragraphs: The paper studies whether a noisy data matrix contains a rank-one signal, a structured component built from a single pair of directions. Its models extend spiked Wishart matrices. The objective is signal detection: deciding whether structure is present within the noise.

The authors show that transforming individual matrix entries before applying principal component analysis can improve that method when the noise is non-Gaussian. As part of the analysis, they prove a sharp transition in the behavior of the largest eigenvalues of spiked rectangular matrices. This extends the BBP transition and characterizes a change in the spectral behavior relevant to detecting a signal.

They also propose a computationally inexpensive hypothesis test based on linear spectral statistics, which summarize information from eigenvalues. In the Gaussian-noise setting studied, the test minimizes the combined probability of false positives and false negatives. The findings distinguish two contributions: preprocessing can improve principal component analysis for non-Gaussian noise, while the stated testing optimality applies when noise is Gaussian.
icml-2021-detection-of-signal-in-the-spi.tldr: The paper improves spectral signal detection through non-Gaussian preprocessing and develops a low-cost test with Gaussian-noise optimality.

paragraphs: Recommender systems can use graph information alongside observed ratings to estimate users' underlying preferences. The paper investigates how much rating data is needed to do this reliably. Its starting point is that earlier theoretical guarantees relied on restrictive assumptions about preference values and the structure of user groups.

The authors introduce a model allowing arbitrary discrete preference values and multiple user clusters. Within this model, they fully characterize the optimal sample complexity: the amount of data needed for the estimation problem. They also construct a computationally efficient algorithm that attains this statistical requirement, connecting a fundamental data limit to an achievable method.

The contribution therefore broadens the setting in which graph-assisted recommendation has matching sample-complexity guarantees. It does not remove the model's discrete-valued and clustered structure; it relaxes particular restrictions within that structure. The authors additionally report robustness to model errors and better prediction performance than existing algorithms on both synthetic and real data, providing empirical support alongside the theoretical characterization.
icml-2021-discrete-valued-latent-prefere.tldr: A broader model of graph-assisted recommendation admits an efficient estimator that matches the optimal sample complexity.

paragraphs: Off-policy reinforcement learning uses experience generated by one behavior policy to learn about another. Combining this with temporal-difference updates and function approximation can cause instability, a combination often called the deadly triad. Emphatic temporal-difference methods address this by weighting learning updates and have a convergence guarantee in the linear setting.

This paper investigates how to carry emphatic methods into deep reinforcement learning. A straightforward adaptation performs poorly when applied to popular algorithms that use forward-view, multistep returns. The authors therefore derive new emphatic algorithms tailored to that form of learning rather than relying on the direct adaptation.

The new methods show noticeable benefits on small problems designed to expose temporal-difference instability. The authors also observe improved performance when using them at scale on classic Atari games. These results support adapting the weighting mechanism to the update structure used by deep agents. The stated convergence guarantee belongs to the linear predecessor; the reported evidence for the deep variants consists of these experimental improvements.
icml-2021-emphatic-algorithms-for-deep-r.tldr: New emphatic update rules tailored to multistep deep reinforcement learning improve performance on instability-focused problems and Atari games.

paragraphs: Causal estimation often assumes that a complete causal graph is already known. Observational data, however, may identify only a Markov equivalence class: multiple causal structures compatible with the available evidence. This paper studies estimation when that ambiguity is represented by a partial ancestral graph, or PAG.

The authors develop a general procedure for effects that are identifiable from a PAG. Their complete identification algorithm derives an influence function for any such effect. That function then supports construction of a double, or debiased, machine-learning estimator, connecting graphical identification to an actual estimation method.

The estimator is designed to be robust to model misspecification and biases in estimating nuisance functions, the supporting quantities needed to estimate the causal effect. This permits modern machine-learning methods within the estimation process. Simulations support the theoretical results. The contribution fills a step between learning a graph equivalence class and estimating causal effects, while retaining the essential condition that the requested effect must be identifiable from the PAG.
icml-2021-estimating-identifiable-causal.tldr: The paper connects causal identification from partial ancestral graphs to debiased machine-learning estimation for every identifiable effect.

paragraphs: In logistic bandit problems, decisions depend on estimating rewards and understanding the uncertainty in those estimates. This paper improves fixed-design confidence bounds for the linear logistic model. Earlier bounds depended directly on the inverse of the smallest reward variance across all arms, a quantity that can grow exponentially with the unknown parameter's norm.

Using self-concordant analysis of logistic loss, the authors replace that direct worst-case dependence with a bound tied to the reward variance of the particular arm being assessed. This makes the confidence statement more specific to the arm instead of letting a single global minimum variance determine the bound.

The authors apply the result to both pure exploration, where learning is the objective, and regret minimization, where choices must also earn rewards. Both applications improve stated performance guarantees. A complementary lower bound shows that inverse-minimum-variance dependence still arises for a family of pure-exploration instances. The improvement therefore refines uncertainty analysis without claiming that this difficult dependence disappears from every related learning problem.
icml-2021-improved-confidence-bounds-for.tldr: Arm-specific variance yields sharper logistic confidence bounds and better bandit guarantees, while a lower bound preserves a worst-case dependence for some exploration problems.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning must learn from an existing dataset without collecting further experience. If that dataset poorly covers some behavior, estimated values can be misleading. The paper studies whether pessimism, which penalizes uncertain value estimates, can provide useful guarantees without assuming sufficient dataset coverage.

The proposed pessimistic value iteration algorithm, PEVI, subtracts an uncertainty penalty during value updates. This reverses the role of the uncertainty bonus used to encourage exploration in online learning. The authors describe the construction as easy to implement and compatible with general function approximators, and establish a data-dependent bound on policy suboptimality for general Markov decision processes.

For linear MDPs, the bound matches an information-theoretic lower bound up to factors involving dimension and horizon. This supports a qualified minimax interpretation of the method's efficiency. The analysis also explains how pessimism removes a form of spurious correlation associated with poorly covered trajectories that are uninformative for the optimal policy. The guarantee depends on the available data rather than requiring broad coverage in advance.
icml-2021-is-pessimism-provably-efficien.tldr: Pessimistic value iteration provides data-dependent offline-RL guarantees without sufficient coverage assumptions and approaches a lower bound in linear MDPs.

paragraphs: The paper develops a probabilistic latent-variable model for data described through pairwise dissimilarities. Its aim is to learn a representation that respects both observed distances and the data's topology, meaning its underlying pattern of connectivity. The representation is tied to the geometry of the manifold generated by the model.

The authors use Riemannian geometry to define a stochastic distance measure in latent space. Locally, those uncertain distances are modeled with Nakagami distributions. Through a censoring process, the model seeks agreement between these stochastic distances and observed distances along a neighborhood graph, linking geometric uncertainty to the relationships supplied by the data.

Inference uses a variational method based on pairwise distance observations. This makes the dissimilarity information central to learning the latent representation, while the neighborhood graph supplies the local relationships used for distance matching. The authors demonstrate that the resulting manifolds can encode invariances. The contribution brings distance preservation, topology, and probabilistic geometric modeling into one latent-variable framework.
icml-2021-isometric-gaussian-process-lat.tldr: A probabilistic latent-variable model uses manifold geometry and uncertain distances to represent dissimilarity data while respecting topology and encoding invariances.

paragraphs: A reinforcement-learning policy trained in simulated environments can perform poorly when the target environment differs. Randomizing training environments can improve average performance, yet leave difficult environments insufficiently addressed. This paper targets average and worst-case performance together, treating both as relevant to generalization.

The authors derive a lower bound on a policy's worst-case performance in terms of its expected performance. They use this relationship to formulate a joint optimization over the policy and the distribution used to sample training environments. For the iterative solution of that optimization problem, they prove that worst-case performance improves monotonically.

The practical algorithm developed from this analysis is called monotonic robust policy optimization, or MRPO. On several robot-control tasks, it generally improves both average and worst-case performance in the source training environments. It also improves generalization across the reported evaluations on some unseen testing environments. These experiments support the practical approach, while the monotonic-improvement theorem concerns the iterative optimization formulation established in the analysis.
icml-2021-monotonic-robust-policy-optimi.tldr: MRPO jointly optimizes policies and environment sampling to improve robustness, guided by a bound connecting expected and worst-case performance.

paragraphs: Thompson sampling is widely used for sequential decisions because it is simple to implement and has strong empirical performance. The paper addresses a theoretical question left open by that success: whether a Thompson-sampling-style algorithm can attain the best possible worst-case regret rate for multi-armed bandits.

The proposed method, MOTS, modifies Thompson sampling by adaptively truncating the sampling result associated with the chosen arm at each time step. This is a targeted change to the sampling procedure. The authors prove that it achieves regret of order the square root of T times K, where T is the decision horizon and K is the number of arms.

That rate is minimax optimal for finite horizons, matching the best achievable worst-case order. The paper also proves asymptotic regret optimality as the horizon grows without bound. These are complementary guarantees about finite-horizon worst-case behavior and long-run performance. The contribution establishes both for the proposed variant, resolving the stated minimax question for Thompson-sampling-type algorithms.
icml-2021-mots-minimax-optimal-thompson-.tldr: MOTS adds adaptive truncation to Thompson sampling and achieves both minimax-optimal finite-horizon regret and asymptotically optimal regret.

paragraphs: The paper examines how an overfitted model can still predict unseen data accurately. Its setting is specific: minimum Euclidean-norm fitting solutions for the neural tangent kernel model of a two-layer ReLU network without bias terms. The analysis asks how generalization changes with network width, training-set size, and the target function.

For a class of learnable target functions, the authors derive a generalization-error upper bound that approaches a small limiting value as the number of neurons grows without bound. That limiting value decreases further as more training examples become available. Thus, increasing width does not force the bound to deteriorate indefinitely for this function class.

For functions outside that class, the authors establish a lower bound that remains nonzero even when both width and sample size are large. The target function therefore plays a decisive role in the conclusions. The resulting behavior differs from the double-descent patterns associated with other overparameterized linear models using simple Fourier or Gaussian features.
icml-2021-on-the-generalization-power-of.tldr: Generalization bounds for overfitted two-layer NTK models depend on the target function, with favorable limits for one class and persistent error outside it.

paragraphs: Online selection requires making decisions as items arrive, before the full instance is known. This paper uses predictions to restrict which instances an adversary may present. It assumes that the eventual instance is consistent with those predictions, then seeks the best worst-case performance over all instances satisfying that restriction.

This assumption changes the role of prediction quality. Instead of designing around arbitrarily inaccurate predictions, the analysis treats consistency as part of the problem definition. For selecting a single item, the authors give an optimal algorithm when arrival order is adversarial and an improved algorithm when arrivals are random, the setting associated with the secretary problem.

The paper also studies online edge-weighted bipartite matching and extends the classical Water-filling and Ranking algorithms. These extensions achieve improved competitive ratios, which compare an online algorithm's performance with an optimal solution that knows the full instance. The results show how prediction-based restrictions can strengthen worst-case guarantees, with the guarantees applying to the assumed class of prediction-consistent instances.
icml-2021-online-selection-problems-agai.tldr: Assuming instances agree with predictions enables stronger worst-case guarantees for online item selection and bipartite matching.

paragraphs: The paper studies best-arm identification when arms arrive in a stream and can be accessed only while stored in limited memory. Each arm has an unknown mean reward, with rewards bounded between zero and one. The challenge combines statistical uncertainty with restrictions on retaining and revisiting candidate arms.

For approximate top-k identification, the authors give a single-pass algorithm using single-arm memory. With probability at least 1−delta, it returns k arms whose means are no more than epsilon below the kth-best mean. Its optimal sample complexity is of order n divided by epsilon squared, multiplied by log(k/delta), extending the earlier single-best-arm setting.

For identifying the exact best arm, they again use single-arm memory but allow multiple passes. Their algorithm has nearly instance-optimal sample complexity and needs a number of passes logarithmic in the inverse gap between the best and second-best means. The two results distinguish approximate selection in one pass from exact identification, where closer leading means affect the stated pass bound.
icml-2021-optimal-streaming-algorithms-f.tldr: Single-arm-memory streaming algorithms achieve optimal approximate top-k sampling and nearly instance-optimal exact best-arm identification with multiple passes.

paragraphs: A model's Lipschitz constant bounds how strongly its output can change relative to a change in its input. This paper develops a scalable way to certify an upper bound on that quantity for generative models. The focus includes networks with large output dimensions, where the certification problem must account for many output directions.

The authors relate the desired bound to the largest norm among attainable vector-Jacobian products. These products describe directional sensitivity through the model's derivatives. Rather than representing their full attainable set exactly, the method builds convex approximations layer by layer using geometric objects called zonotopes.

The approach generalizes and improves earlier work based on zonotope transformers and extends it to high-dimensional outputs. The authors report efficient, tight bounds for small networks and demonstrate scalability to generative models using VAE and DCGAN architectures. The result is an upper-bound certificate: it constrains possible sensitivity, while the reported tightness and scalability describe different aspects of the method's performance at different network scales.
icml-2021-provable-lipschitz-certificati.tldr: Layerwise zonotope approximations provide provable Lipschitz upper bounds that extend to generative networks with large outputs.

paragraphs: Some applications need a low-rank approximation after applying a function separately to every matrix entry. An important example transforms each value into log(1 plus its absolute value). Explicitly storing the matrix and repeatedly processing its entries is expensive, motivating algorithms that work with much smaller memory.

Prior work achieved a compact-memory factorization using three passes over the input. This paper resolves the stated open question of doing so in a single pass, for the same class of transformation functions. Memory remains n times a polynomial in inverse accuracy, target rank, and log n, rather than requiring storage of all n squared entries.

The error guarantee also improves. Its leading term is the optimal rank-k squared Frobenius error without the earlier factor of ten. The additive term scales with the transformed matrix's squared Frobenius norm, replacing a larger quantity based on summing row lengths before squaring. The method therefore improves both input-access requirements and the stated approximation bound within the studied function class.
icml-2021-single-pass-entrywise-transfor.tldr: A single-pass algorithm approximates entrywise-transformed matrices with compact memory and a sharper error guarantee than the previous three-pass method.

paragraphs: Column subset selection represents a matrix using a selection of its actual columns. This paper studies entrywise p-norm error for p from one up to, but excluding, two, a loss often regarded as more robust to noise than Frobenius error. The setting has many more columns than rows.

The authors provide a single-pass streaming algorithm with memory optimal up to a logarithmic factor. Its approximation factor relative to the best size-k column subset is k raised to 1/p−1/2, multiplied by polylogarithmic factors in matrix dimensions. The method also extends to a one-round distributed protocol with nearly optimal communication.

The key reduction uses a mixed norm that first measures each column's Euclidean length and then combines those lengths with a p-norm. This enables existing Euclidean coreset constructions to serve the new objective. The paper also gives guarantees for greedy selection under the corresponding mixed norm with p equal to one, offering a practical subroutine. Experiments report significant advantages on real-world data-analysis tasks.
icml-2021-streaming-and-distributed-algo.tldr: Robust column selection gains single-pass and one-round distributed algorithms with approximation guarantees and nearly optimal resource use.

paragraphs: The paper addresses private model training when data remains distributed across user devices. Its system adds noise on each device and uses secure aggregation so that the server receives only the noisy sum. The aim is to make the privacy mechanism work together with the numerical representation and aggregation process used in the system.

The method discretizes data and adds discrete Gaussian noise before aggregation. The authors develop a privacy analysis for sums of these noise variables. They also analyze quantization, which maps values to finite precision, and modular arithmetic, which governs how represented values are summed within a bounded numerical range.

These components matter jointly because communication, privacy, and accuracy impose competing demands. The theoretical guarantees characterize that tension rather than treating numerical implementation as separate from privacy. Extensive experiments show that the system can essentially match the accuracy of central differential privacy while using fewer than sixteen bits per value. This is an empirical accuracy comparison supported by an end-to-end analysis of the distributed mechanism.
icml-2021-the-distributed-discrete-gauss.tldr: A distributed discrete-Gaussian privacy system combines on-device noise and secure aggregation while empirically approaching central-private accuracy below sixteen bits per value.

paragraphs: Cooperating agents may benefit from developing distinct patterns of behavior, creating opportunities for a division of labor. This paper proposes emergence of individuality, or EOI, as a way to encourage such differentiation in multi-agent reinforcement learning. Its mechanism rewards agents for becoming recognizable from their observations.

EOI trains a probabilistic classifier to predict which agent produced a given observation. An agent receives an intrinsic reward when the classifier correctly identifies it. This encourages agents to revisit observations associated with themselves. Training the classifier on those observations strengthens the identification signal, producing a reinforcing interaction between behavior and classification.

The authors add two regularizers that improve the classifier's ability to distinguish agents and thereby strengthen the intrinsic reward. They implement EOI on top of popular multi-agent learning algorithms and report better performance than existing methods across varied cooperative scenarios. The experiments support individuality as a useful training incentive in those settings, without requiring the method to assign a predefined role to each agent.
icml-2021-the-emergence-of-individuality.tldr: EOI encourages distinctive agent behavior through identification-based intrinsic rewards and improves performance in tested cooperative multi-agent settings.

paragraphs: The paper studies how much data is needed to find a nearly optimal policy for an infinite-horizon Markov decision process evaluated by average reward. The learner has access to a generative model that supplies samples. The analysis concerns sample complexity, connecting the required data to accuracy and how quickly the system mixes.

The main assumption is that every policy's transition matrix has mixing time at most t_mix. Under this condition, the authors provide an algorithm using roughly t_mix times epsilon to the power of minus three samples per state-action pair, with logarithmic factors suppressed. The sampling is oblivious, using the sampling framework specified in the result.

A lower bound shows that linear dependence on mixing time is unavoidable in the worst case for algorithms using oblivious samples. This establishes tightness of that particular dependence, without claiming that every factor in the upper bound is matched. The proofs connect average-reward problems to discounted MDPs, providing a relationship the authors suggest may have further theoretical uses.
icml-2021-towards-tight-bounds-on-the-sa.tldr: New average-reward MDP bounds establish linear mixing-time dependence as sufficient and worst-case necessary for oblivious sampling under the stated assumptions.

paragraphs: Recurrent networks are commonly trained by propagating errors backward through a sequence. Over long sequences, gradients can grow excessively or shrink, making learning difficult. This paper changes the training procedure itself through forward propagation through time, or FPTT, rather than addressing the problem only through network architecture.

FPTT updates network parameters at each time step by optimizing an instantaneous risk function. Its regularization penalty evolves using losses observed earlier in the sequence, allowing earlier learning signals to affect the current update. The proposed construction allows parameter updates to converge to a stationary solution of the empirical recurrent-network objective.

The authors consider both sequence-to-sequence problems and problems where loss is supplied at the end. Experiments show FPTT outperforming back-propagation through time on several established benchmarks, including enabling LSTM architectures to handle long-range dependencies. The theoretical destination is a stationary solution, rather than a claimed global optimum, while the benchmark results provide empirical evidence for the training procedure's usefulness.
icml-2021-training-recurrent-neural-netw.tldr: FPTT trains recurrent networks through sequential updates with a dynamic regularizer, supporting stationary convergence and improved benchmark performance.
